title: Nosebleeds, Anaemia and Spots on the Lips / Think Hidden Lung and Brain Lesions

blocks.text: Nosebleeds, Anaemia and Spots on the Lips / Think Hidden Lung and Brain Lesions

AMaC MRCP PACES · R3-25 · Consultation · PACES Station 5 (less acute), consultation encounter · Skills A, B, C, D, E, F, G (all seven) · 20 min: 15 min with the patient, then 5 min of examiner questions; warning at 13 min · Guidelines: Second International Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Management of HHT (Ann Intern Med 2020;173:989-1001), including the recommendations retained from the First International Guidelines (J Med Genet 2011;48:73-87) for pulmonary arteriovenous malformations and brain vascular malformations · Related AMaC: Consultation: iron-deficiency anaemia (existing AMaC station)

Dear Doctor, a 47-year-old nursery nurse. Years of nosebleeds, now several a week. Hb 98 g/L, ferritin low despite iron tablets. Her father had nosebleeds and died of a stroke at 52. Please assess and advise.
Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to the patient.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. Recurrent spontaneous nosebleeds, telangiectasia and family history point to hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia; the lesson is to look for hidden lung and brain lesions.

The Examiner Trap. She asks only about the nosebleeds. Candidates treat the nose and the anaemia and stop. Pass: recognise suspected HHT, arrange specialist screening and family assessment. Fail: treat the nose only.

rows: Nosebleeds alone, or a systemic disease? Get the story.
"How often do the nosebleeds come? Any breathlessness, headaches, black stools or family history?"
Introduce, consent, ask about pain; epistaxis, bowel bleeding, dyspnoea, neurology, family, anticoagulants.
Look for telangiectasia and its effects.
"May I look at your lips, tongue, fingers and nose, and listen to your chest?"
Lips, tongue, fingertips, nose, pallor, clubbing, cyanosis, chest bruit, oxygen saturation, liver bruit.
"These spots may be a family condition affecting blood vessels, including in the lung and brain."
Current oxygenation and warning symptoms; expedited lung AVM screening; moisturising nasal care; iron; brain MRI; family testing.
Share the plan; find her worry.
Explain tests, options and family implications; safety net; check understanding.
Examines without consent; ignores a nosebleed or breathlessness
Introduces, consents, asks about discomfort, covers her
Offers tissues and a chaperone, and thanks her
No family or lung or neurological history
Asks frequency, bowel bleeding, breathlessness, headaches, family history and drugs
Also asks about strokes, abscesses, pregnancies, blood thinners and the effect on work
Acknowledges worry; asks what concerns her
Finds the fear for her daughter and for a stroke like her father's, and answers honestly
Lip, tongue and finger telangiectasia, pallor, oxygen saturation; reports them
Adds clubbing, cyanosis, chest and liver bruits and states negatives: no neurology, no hepatomegaly
Applies the Curaçao criteria; two confirmed criteria mean possible HHT, three mean definite. A relative with nosebleeds alone does not fulfil the confirmed-family criterion
Treats the nose only; no lung or brain screening
Screens for pulmonary and brain lesions, with lung screening expedited because she is breathless with a saturation of 94 per cent; treats iron deficiency; moisturising nasal care

Adds oral then intravenous iron, anticoagulation cautions, referral to a specialist centre and a safety net: same-day assessment for coughing up blood, new weakness, speech or vision change, fever with headache, or worsening breathlessness
Gives instructions without options; ignores family
Explains options; offers family testing; checks understanding
Covers genetic testing for her daughter, benefits, risks, alternatives and what happens if lesions are found

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. High-performance includes the pass behaviours. This station-specific grid is an AMaC teaching framework mapped to PACES skills, not an official mark scheme. Consent, hand hygiene, dignity and an appropriate chaperone are baseline professional practice.
Who you are. A 47-year-old nursery nurse. Tired, practical, worried about her daughter. Lives with your husband and daughter. Never smoked; alcohol rarely. No recent travel.
Opening line. "I'm sick of these nosebleeds and I'm always tired."
Volunteered. Nosebleeds several times a week for years; tired; iron tablets upset your stomach.

Only if asked. Little red spots on your lips and fingers for years. Black stools sometimes. Breathless on stairs lately; no coughing up of blood, no fever. Occasional headaches, no fits or weakness. Your father had nosebleeds and died of a stroke at 52; a brother has nosebleeds. Your daughter, 19, has nosebleeds. Medicines: ferrous fumarate tablets (which upset your stomach), nothing else; no blood thinners. No allergies. You drive normally and have had no faints.
Hidden concern. You fear that your daughter has the same illness and that you may have a stroke like your father. Reveal only if asked what worries you most.
Your questions. "Is it hereditary?" "Will my daughter get it?" "Do I need a brain scan?" "Can the bleeding be stopped?"
How you react. Good handling: you agree to tests and ask for your daughter to be seen. Poor handling: if only the nose is treated you say it will not help.

Findings (released as each step is done). Pale. Multiple small red telangiectasia on lips, tongue and fingertips. Oxygen saturation 94 per cent in air (scenario). No clubbing or cyanosis. Chest clear, no bruit. No liver bruit or hepatomegaly. Neurology normal. Hb 98 g/L, ferritin low (scenario values).

Question ladder. Q1 Diagnosis (R5): hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia. Q2 Features (R5): recurrent spontaneous nosebleeds, telangiectasia, visceral lesions, family history. Q3 Screening (R6): adult pulmonary AVM screening initially by transthoracic contrast echocardiography, expedited through the HHT service because she is breathless with a saturation of 94 per cent (the guideline sets no timescale; haemoptysis, new focal neurology or fever with headache need same-day assessment); chest CT is used when indicated to define lesions; brain MRI for adults with possible or definite HHT (International HHT guidelines). Q4 Anaemia (R6): test for iron deficiency; oral iron first, intravenous if it fails (HHT guideline, anaemia section). Q5 Family (R7): offer assessment and genetic testing to first-degree relatives through the specialist and genetics services; her daughter, who already has nosebleeds, needs assessment (HHT guidelines 2020).
Curveball 1. "She needs blood thinners for a clot." (R6) Safe: bleeding in HHT is not an absolute contraindication; weigh bleeding risk; avoid dual antiplatelet therapy where possible.

Curveball 2. "Nasal packing." (R6) Safe: for an acute significant bleed, give first aid and urgent ENT assessment; use atraumatic packing if needed. Moisturising therapy is first-line prevention for recurrent epistaxis.
Curveball 3. "She has a brain abscess." (R6) Safe: urgent neuroimaging and neurosurgical advice; a lung lesion may be the route.
Curveball 4. "She declines the brain scan." (R7) Safe: capacity present; explain risks; revisit.

CANDIDATE: What's happened? [R1 Fail] (No family or lung history. [R2 Fail] [R3 Fail])
(Reports telangiectasia without looking. [R4 Fail])
CANDIDATE: They're just nosebleeds. [R5 Fail] Iron tablets and see the ENT clinic. [R6 Fail]
CANDIDATE: That's all. [R7 Fail]
Examiner note: No family history, signs not examined, nose treated alone. Hidden lung and brain lesions go unchecked.
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: Hello. May I examine you? Any discomfort? [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: How often are the nosebleeds? Any breathlessness or headaches? Anyone in the family with nosebleeds? [R2 Pass]
PATIENT: My father died of a stroke. I'm afraid for my daughter.
CANDIDATE: That's a real worry. What concerns you most? [R3 Pass]
(Inspects lips, tongue and fingers; checks oxygen saturation; finds telangiectasia and pallor. [R4 Pass])
CANDIDATE: This looks like hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia. [R5 Pass]

CANDIDATE: I'll arrange the lung scan quickly because you are breathless and your oxygen level is a little low, screen for brain lesions, treat your iron deficiency and use moisturising nasal care. [R6 Pass]
CANDIDATE: Your daughter can be offered genetic testing. What would you like me to explain further? [R7 Pass]
Examiner note: Safe and clear. Did not name alternatives or discuss intravenous iron and blood thinners.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: Hello. May I examine you? Any discomfort? [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: How often are the nosebleeds? Any breathlessness or headaches? Anyone in the family with nosebleeds? [R2 High]
CANDIDATE: May I offer a chaperone? Here are tissues. [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: Any strokes, abscesses, blood thinners or effect on your work? [R2 High]
PATIENT: I'm afraid my daughter has it too.
CANDIDATE: Thank you for telling me. We'll test and help her too. [R3 High]
(Inspects lips, tongue and fingers; checks oxygen saturation; finds telangiectasia and pallor. [R4 High])
(No clubbing or cyanosis; no chest or liver bruit; neurology normal. [R4 High])

CANDIDATE: The pattern strongly suggests HHT. Recurrent epistaxis and telangiectasia are established; the relatives need assessment and visceral lesions are not yet confirmed. I'd exclude clotting and liver disease. [R5 High]

CANDIDATE: I'll arrange the lung scan quickly because you are breathless and your oxygen level is a little low, screen for brain lesions, treat your iron deficiency and use moisturising nasal care. [R6 High]

CANDIDATE: Transthoracic contrast echocardiography for lung AVMs, with CT when indicated, and a discussion of brain MRI through the HHT centre. Oral iron first, intravenous if it fails. Blood thinners are not forbidden but need care. Referral to a specialist centre. Come in the same day if you cough up blood, have weakness, speech or vision change, fever with headache, or your breathing worsens. [R6 High]
CANDIDATE: Your daughter can have genetic testing; options are testing now or waiting, and testing finds problems early. If a lesion is found a specialist will advise. [R7 High]
Examiner note: Answered the fear for her daughter and covered family testing.
R6: Treating the nose alone leaves possible lung and brain lesions unchecked.
R2: No family or lung history misses the diagnosis.
R4: Reporting telangiectasia not examined shows signs were assumed.
R5: Calling them simple nosebleeds ignores the lips, anaemia and family history.
R7: Ignoring her daughter leaves the family at risk.
"Is anyone else in the family affected?"
"Let me look at your lips and fingers."
"I'd check for hidden lesions in the lung and brain."

Second International HHT guideline (2020): moisturising topical therapy for epistaxis; test all adults for iron deficiency and anaemia; oral iron first, intravenous iron if it fails; bleeding is not an absolute contraindication to antithrombotics.

Adult pulmonary AVM screening initially uses transthoracic contrast echocardiography; CT characterises lesions when indicated. MRI is advised for brain screening in adults. Genetic testing is offered to relatives; asymptomatic children of an affected parent are treated as having possible HHT unless testing excludes it.

She has two established Curaçao criteria: spontaneous recurrent epistaxis and characteristic telangiectasia. Relatives with nosebleeds are suggestive, but the family criterion requires a first-degree relative with confirmed HHT; refer as possible or strongly suspected HHT pending AVM or genetic confirmation. Arrange adult lung AVM screening, discuss brain MRI and offer liver vascular-malformation screening through a specialist centre. Iron intolerance supports IV iron assessment. Black stools may be iron-related but need evaluation for gastrointestinal blood loss. New breathlessness with a saturation of 94 per cent needs prompt assessment, not a routine wait: anaemia may explain it, but a pulmonary AVM must be excluded. For documented pulmonary AVMs, discuss antibiotic cover for procedures that cause bacteraemia, meticulous avoidance of air in intravenous lines, and avoiding scuba diving.
THINK: HHT; hidden lung and brain lesions.
SAY: "These spots may be a family condition affecting blood vessels."
DO: Lips, tongue, fingers; saturation; lung and brain screening; iron.
NUMBERS: Hb 98 g/L, saturation 94 per cent (scenario).
TRAP: Treating the nose only.
FINISH: Expedite lung screening; offer family testing; safety net.

International HHT guidelines: pulmonary arteriovenous malformations (First International Guidelines 2009, retained in the Second International Guidelines 2020). Adult screening with contrast echocardiography and advice. https://hhtguidelines.org/avm/

International HHT guidelines: brain vascular malformations (First International Guidelines 2009, retained in the Second International Guidelines 2020). MRI screening in adults with possible or definite HHT. https://hhtguidelines.org/brain/

Second International HHT Guidelines (Ann Intern Med 2020;173:989-1001): table of recommendations. Epistaxis; anaemia; antithrombotics; liver screening; family and genetic assessment. https://hhtguidelines.org/table/
